\proofstep
  {FABL.two_mul_exp_neg_two_mul_condorcetConstant_sq_le}
  {context}
  {Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}
  {pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p225-b005,
    pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p237-b008}
For every $\varepsilon>0$, there is a constant $C\ge0$ such that
$2e^{-2C^2}\le\varepsilon$ and, for every natural number $m$ satisfying
$C/\sqrt{2m+1}\le1/2$, the biased minus-probability polynomial of majority on $2m+1$
bits is at most $\varepsilon$ at bias parameter $p=1/2-C/\sqrt{2m+1}$, and is at least
$1-\varepsilon$ at $p=1/2+C/\sqrt{2m+1}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Existence of subsets of each size]
\lean{FABL.powersetCard_univ_nonempty}
\label{FABL.powersetCard_univ_nonempty}
\leanok
\difficulty{3}
For every natural number $n$ and every integer $k$ with $0\le k\le n$, the family of
$k$-element subsets of an $n$-element set is nonempty.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Uniform Shapley subset distribution]
\lean{FABL.shapleySubsetPMF}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p239-b009}
\label{FABL.shapleySubsetPMF}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.powersetCard_univ_nonempty}
For each natural number $n$, let $S$ be a random subset of $\\{0,1,\\ldots,n-1\\}$. Its
distribution is obtained by choosing a size uniformly from $0$ through $n$, then
choosing uniformly among all subsets of that size.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Shapley distribution on the Boolean cube]
\lean{FABL.shapleyF₂PMF}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.F₂Cube, FABL.f₂CubeEquivFinset, FABL.shapleySubsetPMF}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p239-b009}
For each natural number $n$, define a probability mass function on the $n$-dimensional
Boolean cube by transporting the Shapley subset distribution on subsets of
$\text{Fin}(n)$ through the inverse of the correspondence between subsets and functions
from $\text{Fin}(n)$ to $\bbr/\bbr 2\bbz$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Subset cardinality index]
\lean{FABL.subsetCardIndex}
\label{FABL.subsetCardIndex}
\leanok
For a subset $S$ of $\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$, its subset cardinality index is the element of
$\{0,\ldots,n\}$ equal to $|S|$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Probability of a subset of fixed size]
\lean{FABL.shapleySubsetPMF_apply}
\label{FABL.shapleySubsetPMF_apply}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.shapleySubsetPMF, FABL.subsetCardIndex}
\difficulty{5}
Let $n$ be a nonnegative integer and let $S$ be a subset of an $n$-element set. Under
the distribution obtained by choosing a size uniformly from $0,1,\ldots,n$ and then
choosing uniformly among subsets of that size, the probability of selecting $S$ is
$1/((n+1)\binom{n}{|S|})$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Real probability of a subset]
\lean{FABL.shapleySubsetPMF_apply_toReal}
\label{FABL.shapleySubsetPMF_apply_toReal}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.shapleySubsetPMF, FABL.shapleySubsetPMF_apply}
\difficulty{3}
Let $n$ be a nonnegative integer and let $S$ be a subset of an $n$-element set. Under
the distribution obtained by choosing a size uniformly from $0,1,\ldots,n$ and then
choosing uniformly among subsets of that size, the probability of selecting $S$, viewed
as a real number, is $1/((n+1)\binom{n}{|S|})$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Shapley expectation]
\lean{FABL.shapleyExpectation}
\label{FABL.shapleyExpectation}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.pmfExpectation, FABL.shapleySubsetPMF}
For a function $f$ from the subsets of $\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$ to $\mathbb R$, its Shapley
expectation is the expectation of $f$ under the Shapley subset probability mass function
on those subsets.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Expectation under the Shapley cube distribution]
\lean{FABL.pmfExpectation_shapleyF₂PMF}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.F₂Cube, FABL.f₂CubeEquivFinset, FABL.pmfExpectation, FABL.pmfExpectation_map, FABL.shapleyExpectation, FABL.shapleyF₂PMF}
\difficulty{1}
Let $n$ be a nonnegative integer, identify vectors in $(\mathbb{F}_2)^n$ with subsets of
$\{1,\ldots,n\}$ by their supports, and let $f:(\mathbb{F}_2)^n\to\mathbb{R}$. Choose an
integer $k$ uniformly from $0$ through $n$, then choose uniformly a subset of size $k$
and take its indicator vector. The expectation of $f$ under this vector distribution
equals the expectation of the function on subsets that sends $S$ to the value of $f$ at
the indicator vector of $S$, under the corresponding subset distribution.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Expectation by cardinality and subset]
\lean{FABL.shapleyExpectation_eq_uniform_cardinality_then_subset}
\label{FABL.shapleyExpectation_eq_uniform_cardinality_then_subset}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.pmfExpectation, FABL.pmfExpectation_bind, FABL.powersetCard_univ_nonempty, FABL.shapleyExpectation, FABL.shapleySubsetPMF}
\difficulty{1}
For any real-valued function on the subsets of an $n$-element set, its Shapley
expectation equals the expectation obtained by first choosing a cardinality uniformly
from $0,1,\ldots,n$ and then choosing uniformly among the subsets of that cardinality.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Shapley value]
\lean{FABL.shapleyValue}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p240-b002}
\label{FABL.shapleyValue}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.shapleyExpectation}
For a function $f$ from subsets of an $n$-element set to the real numbers and an element
$i$, define its Shapley value at $i$ to be the Shapley expectation of the marginal
difference $f(S\cup\{i\})-f(S\setminus\{i\})$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Subset point indicator]
\lean{FABL.subsetPointIndicator}
\label{FABL.subsetPointIndicator}
\leanok
Let $n$ be a natural number, and let $A$ and $S$ be subsets of $\\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$. The
subset point indicator at $A$ is $1$ if $S=A$ and $0$ otherwise.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Characterizing equality after insertion]
\lean{FABL.insert_eq_fixed_iff}
\label{FABL.insert_eq_fixed_iff}
\leanok
\difficulty{4}
For finite sets $S,A\subseteq\mathrm{Fin}(n)$ and $i\in\mathrm{Fin}(n)$, inserting $i$
into $S$ gives $A$ if and only if $i\in A$ and either $S=A$ or $S=A\setminus\{i\}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Characterization of finite-set erasure]
\lean{FABL.erase_eq_fixed_iff}
\label{FABL.erase_eq_fixed_iff}
\leanok
\difficulty{4}
Let $n$ be a nonnegative integer, let $i$ be an element of $\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$, and let
$S$ and $A$ be subsets of that finite index set. Then deleting $i$ from $S$ yields $A$
if and only if $i\notin A$ and either $S=A$ or $S=A\cup\{i\}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Expectation of an inserted-set indicator]
\lean{FABL.shapleyExpectation_pointIndicator_insert}
\label{FABL.shapleyExpectation_pointIndicator_insert}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.insert_eq_fixed_iff, FABL.pmfExpectation, FABL.shapleyExpectation, FABL.shapleySubsetPMF, FABL.subsetPointIndicator}
\difficulty{5}
Let $A$ be a subset of an $n$-element set and let $i$ be an element of that set. The
Shapley expectation of the indicator that inserting $i$ into the sampled subset gives
$A$ is the sum of the Shapley probabilities of $A$ and $A\setminus\{i\}$ when $i\in A$,
and is $0$ when $i\notin A$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Expectation of an erased-set indicator]
\lean{FABL.shapleyExpectation_pointIndicator_erase}
\label{FABL.shapleyExpectation_pointIndicator_erase}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.erase_eq_fixed_iff, FABL.pmfExpectation, FABL.shapleyExpectation, FABL.shapleySubsetPMF, FABL.subsetPointIndicator}
\difficulty{5}
Let $A$ be a subset of an $n$-element set and let $i$ be an element of that set. The
Shapley expectation of the indicator that the subset obtained by deleting $i$ equals $A$
is the sum of the Shapley probabilities of $A$ and $A\cup\{i\}$ when $i\notin A$, and is
$0$ when $i\in A$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Shapley value of a subset indicator]
\lean{FABL.shapleyValue_subsetPointIndicator}
\label{FABL.shapleyValue_subsetPointIndicator}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.pmfExpectation_sub_general, FABL.shapleyExpectation, FABL.shapleyExpectation_pointIndicator_erase, FABL.shapleyExpectation_pointIndicator_insert, FABL.shapleySubsetPMF, FABL.shapleyValue, FABL.subsetPointIndicator}
\difficulty{3}
Let $n$ be a natural number, let $A$ be a subset of an $n$-element set, and let $i$ be
an element of that set. For the game that is $1$ exactly at coalition $A$ and $0$ at
every other coalition, its Shapley value at $i$ is the sum of the probabilities of $A$
and $A\setminus\{i\}$ under the random-subset distribution if $i\in A$; if $i\notin A$,
it is the negative of the sum of the probabilities of $A$ and $A\cup\{i\}$ under that
distribution.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Shapley layer weight]
\lean{FABL.shapleyLayerWeight}
\label{FABL.shapleyLayerWeight}
\leanok
For natural numbers $n$ and $k$, the Shapley layer weight is $1/((n+1)\binom{n}{k})$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Subset probability equals its layer weight]
\lean{FABL.shapleySubsetPMF_apply_toReal_eq_layerWeight}
\label{FABL.shapleySubsetPMF_apply_toReal_eq_layerWeight}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.shapleyLayerWeight, FABL.shapleySubsetPMF, FABL.shapleySubsetPMF_apply_toReal}
\difficulty{1}
Let $n$ be a nonnegative integer and let $S$ be a subset of an $n$-element set. Under
the distribution obtained by choosing a size uniformly from $0,1,\ldots,n$ and then
choosing uniformly among subsets of that size, the probability of selecting $S$, viewed
as a real number, equals its Shapley layer weight, namely $1/((n+1)\binom{n}{|S|})$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Point indicator Shapley sum]
\lean{FABL.sum_shapleyValue_subsetPointIndicator_eq_layerExpression}
\label{FABL.sum_shapleyValue_subsetPointIndicator_eq_layerExpression}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.shapleyLayerWeight, FABL.shapleySubsetPMF, FABL.shapleySubsetPMF_apply_toReal_eq_layerWeight, FABL.shapleyValue, FABL.shapleyValue_subsetPointIndicator, FABL.subsetPointIndicator}
\difficulty{5}
Let $n$ be a nonnegative integer, let $A\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}$, and let $f_A$ be the
indicator of $A$ among subsets: $f_A(S)=1$ if $S=A$ and $0$ otherwise. Choose $S$ by
first choosing its cardinality uniformly from $0,\ldots,n$, then choosing uniformly
among subsets of that cardinality, and define each element's Shapley value as the
expected difference $f_A(S\cup\{i\})-f_A(S\setminus\{i\})$. Then the sum of these values
is
\[
|A|\bigl(w_n(|A|)+w_n(|A|-1)\bigr)-(n-|A|)\bigl(w_n(|A|)+w_n(|A|+1)\bigr),
\]
where $w_n(k)=1/\bigl((n+1)\binom{n}{k}\bigr)$ for nonnegative integers $k$; the
subtractions in the formula are truncated at zero when used as natural-number arguments
or differences.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Endpoint indicator identity for layer weights]
\lean{FABL.shapleyLayerExpression_eq_endpointIndicators}
\label{FABL.shapleyLayerExpression_eq_endpointIndicators}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.shapleyLayerWeight}
\difficulty{6}
Let $A$ be a subset of an $n$-element set, and write $w(n,k)=1/((n+1)\binom{n}{k})$.
Then
\[
|A|\bigl(w(n,|A|)+w(n,|A|-1)\bigr)-(n-|A|)\bigl(w(n,|A|)+w(n,|A|+1)\bigr)=\mathbf{1}_{A=U}-\mathbf{1}_{A=\varnothing},
\]
where $U$ is the entire ground set and $\mathbf{1}_P$ is $1$ if $P$ holds and $0$
otherwise; the cardinality arguments $|A|-1$ and $|A|+1$ are understood as natural
numbers.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Decomposition by point indicators]
\lean{FABL.subsetPointIndicator_decomposition}
\label{FABL.subsetPointIndicator_decomposition}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.subsetPointIndicator}
\difficulty{4}
For every natural number $n$ and every function $f$ from the finite subsets of
$\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$ to $\mathbb{R}$, $f$ is the sum, over all such subsets $A$, of $f(A)$
times the point indicator of $A$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Additivity of the Shapley value]
\lean{FABL.shapleyValue_add}
\label{FABL.shapleyValue_add}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.pmfExpectation_add_fun, FABL.shapleyExpectation, FABL.shapleyValue}
\difficulty{3}
Let $n$ be a nonnegative integer, let $f$ and $g$ be real-valued functions on the
subsets of an $n$-element set, and let $i$ be an element of that set. The Shapley value
of $f+g$ at $i$ is the sum of the Shapley values of $f$ and $g$ at $i$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Homogeneity of the Shapley value]
\lean{FABL.shapleyValue_smul}
\label{FABL.shapleyValue_smul}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.pmfExpectation_smul_fun, FABL.shapleyExpectation, FABL.shapleyValue}
\difficulty{3}
Let $n$ be a natural number, let $f$ be a real-valued function on the subsets of an
$n$-element set, let $i$ be an element of that set, and let $c\in\mathbb R$. The Shapley
value of the game obtained by multiplying $f$ by $c$ is $c$ times the Shapley value of
$f$ at $i$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Additivity of the Shapley value]
\lean{FABL.shapleyValue_sum}
\label{FABL.shapleyValue_sum}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.pmfExpectation_sum, FABL.shapleyExpectation, FABL.shapleyValue}
\difficulty{3}
Let $n$ be a natural number, let $I$ be a finite type, let $g_j$ be a real-valued
function on the subsets of an $n$-element set for each $j\in I$, and let $i$ be an
element of that set. The Shapley value at $i$ of the pointwise sum of the games $g_j$
equals the sum of their Shapley values at $i$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Expansion by point indicators]
\lean{FABL.shapleyValue_eq_sum_pointIndicators}
\label{FABL.shapleyValue_eq_sum_pointIndicators}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.shapleyValue, FABL.shapleyValue_smul, FABL.shapleyValue_sum, FABL.subsetPointIndicator, FABL.subsetPointIndicator_decomposition}
\difficulty{3}
Let $n$ be a nonnegative integer, let $f$ be a real-valued function on the subsets of an
$n$-element set, and let $i$ be an element of that set. The Shapley value of $f$ at $i$
equals the sum, over all subsets $A$, of $f(A)$ times the Shapley value at $i$ of the
indicator function of the singleton collection containing $A$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Sum of Shapley values]
\lean{FABL.sum_shapleyValue}
\label{FABL.sum_shapleyValue}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.shapleyLayerExpression_eq_endpointIndicators, FABL.shapleyValue, FABL.shapleyValue_eq_sum_pointIndicators, FABL.subsetPointIndicator, FABL.sum_shapleyValue_subsetPointIndicator_eq_layerExpression}
\difficulty{4}
Let $n$ be a nonnegative integer and let $f$ be a real-valued function on the subsets of
$\{1,ldots,n\}$. Choose a subset $S$ by first choosing its cardinality uniformly from
$0,\ldots,n$, then choosing uniformly among subsets of that cardinality; for each
element $i$, define its Shapley value as the expected value of
$f(S\cup\{i\})-f(S\setminus\{i\})$. The sum of these values over all $i$ is
$f(\{1,\ldots,n\})-f(\varnothing)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Integral of powers on the unit interval]
\lean{FABL.integral_pow_mul_one_sub_pow}
\label{FABL.integral_pow_mul_one_sub_pow}
\leanok
\difficulty{6}
For natural numbers $k$ and $m$, the integral of $x^k(1-x)^m$ over $[0,1]$ is
\[\int_0^1 x^k(1-x)^m\,dx=\frac{k!\,m!}{(k+m+1)!}.\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Bernoulli subset mass and Shapley weight]
\lean{FABL.integral_bernoulliSubsetMass_eq_shapleyLayerWeight}
\label{FABL.integral_bernoulliSubsetMass_eq_shapleyLayerWeight}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.integral_pow_mul_one_sub_pow, FABL.shapleyLayerWeight}
\difficulty{4}
For natural numbers $n$ and $k$ with $k\le n$, \[\int_0^1
p^k(1-p)^{n-k}\,dp=\frac{1}{(n+1)\binom{n}{k}},\] where $\binom{n}{k}$ is the binomial
coefficient.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Bernoulli subset expectation]
\lean{FABL.bernoulliSubsetExpectation}
\label{FABL.bernoulliSubsetExpectation}
\leanok
For a real number $p$ and a function $f$ from subsets of $\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$ to $\mathbb
R$, the Bernoulli subset expectation is
$\sum_{S\subseteq\{0,\ldots,n-1\}}p^{|S|}(1-p)^{n-|S|}f(S)$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Bernoulli and Shapley subset expectations]
\lean{FABL.integral_bernoulliSubsetExpectation_eq_shapleyExpectation}
\label{FABL.integral_bernoulliSubsetExpectation_eq_shapleyExpectation}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.bernoulliSubsetExpectation, FABL.integral_bernoulliSubsetMass_eq_shapleyLayerWeight, FABL.pmfExpectation, FABL.shapleyExpectation, FABL.shapleySubsetPMF_apply_toReal_eq_layerWeight}
\difficulty{4}
Let $n$ be a natural number and let $f$ be a real-valued function on the subsets of
$\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$. Integrating over $p\in[0,1]$ the expectation of $f(S)$ when each
element is independently included in $S$ with probability $p$ gives the Shapley subset
expectation: the expectation obtained by choosing a cardinality uniformly from $0$
through $n$, then choosing a subset of that cardinality uniformly.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Bernoulli marginal contribution]
\lean{FABL.bernoulliMarginalContribution}
\label{FABL.bernoulliMarginalContribution}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.bernoulliSubsetExpectation}
For a parameter $p\in\mathbb R$, a function $f$ from subsets of $\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$ to
$\mathbb R$, and an index $i\in\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$, define the Bernoulli marginal
contribution to be the Bernoulli subset expectation at parameter $p$ of the function
sending $S$ to $f(S\cup\{i\})-f(S\setminus\{i\})$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Integral formula for the Shapley value]
\lean{FABL.shapleyValue_eq_integral_bernoulliMarginalContribution}
\label{FABL.shapleyValue_eq_integral_bernoulliMarginalContribution}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.bernoulliMarginalContribution, FABL.integral_bernoulliSubsetExpectation_eq_shapleyExpectation, FABL.shapleyValue}
\difficulty{1}
Let $n$ be a nonnegative integer, let $f$ be a real-valued function on the subsets of an
$n$-element set, and let $i$ be an element of that set. The Shapley value of $f$ at $i$
equals the integral from $0$ to $1$ of its Bernoulli marginal contribution as the
inclusion probability varies.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Monotone subset function]
\lean{FABL.IsMonotoneSubsetFunction}
\label{FABL.IsMonotoneSubsetFunction}
\leanok
A function $f$ from subsets of $\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$ to $\mathbb R$ is monotone if,
whenever $S\subseteq T$, one has $f(S)\le f(T)$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Zero-one-valued subset function]
\lean{FABL.HasZeroOneRange}
\label{FABL.HasZeroOneRange}
\leanok
A function $f$ from subsets of $\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$ to $\mathbb R$ has zero-one range if,
for every subset $S$, $f(S)=0$ or $f(S)=1$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Bernoulli subset influence]
\lean{FABL.bernoulliSubsetInfluence}
\label{FABL.bernoulliSubsetInfluence}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.bernoulliSubsetExpectation}
For a parameter $p\in\mathbb R$, a function $f$ from subsets of $\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$ to
$\mathbb R$, and an index $i\in\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$, define the Bernoulli subset influence
at $i$ to be $p(1-p)$ times the Bernoulli subset expectation at parameter $p$ of the
squared marginal difference $\bigl(f(S\cup\{i\})-f(S\setminus\{i\})\bigr)^2$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Squared Marginal Difference]
\lean{FABL.sq_subsetMarginal_eq_self}
\label{FABL.sq_subsetMarginal_eq_self}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.HasZeroOneRange, FABL.IsMonotoneSubsetFunction}
\difficulty{4}
Let $n$ be a natural number, and let $f$ assign a real number to each subset of
$\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$. Suppose $f$ is monotone under inclusion and takes only the values
$0$ and $1$. For every element $i$ and every subset $S$, the square of
$f(S\cup\{i\})-f(S\setminus\{i\})$ equals that difference.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Influence and marginal contribution]
\lean{FABL.bernoulliSubsetInfluence_eq_mul_marginalContribution}
\label{FABL.bernoulliSubsetInfluence_eq_mul_marginalContribution}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.HasZeroOneRange, FABL.IsMonotoneSubsetFunction, FABL.bernoulliMarginalContribution, FABL.bernoulliSubsetExpectation, FABL.bernoulliSubsetInfluence, FABL.sq_subsetMarginal_eq_self}
\difficulty{3}
Let $n$ be a natural number, let $p\in\mathbb R$, and let $f$ be a real-valued function
on the subsets of $\{1,\ldots,n\}$. Suppose $f$ is monotone under inclusion and takes
only the values $0$ and $1$. For each coordinate $i$, its Bernoulli subset influence
equals $p(1-p)$ times its Bernoulli marginal contribution.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Marginal contribution and influence]
\lean{FABL.bernoulliMarginalContribution_eq_influence_div}
\label{FABL.bernoulliMarginalContribution_eq_influence_div}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.HasZeroOneRange, FABL.IsMonotoneSubsetFunction, FABL.bernoulliMarginalContribution, FABL.bernoulliSubsetInfluence, FABL.bernoulliSubsetInfluence_eq_mul_marginalContribution}
\difficulty{3}
Let $n$ be a natural number, let $p\in(0,1)$, and let $f$ be a real-valued function on
the subsets of $\{1,\ldots,n\}$. Suppose $f$ is monotone under inclusion and takes only
the values $0$ and $1$. For each coordinate $i$, its Bernoulli marginal contribution at
parameter $p$ equals its Bernoulli subset influence divided by $p(1-p)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Integral formula under monotonicity and Boolean range]
\lean{FABL.shapleyValue_eq_integral_normalizedInfluence}
\label{FABL.shapleyValue_eq_integral_normalizedInfluence}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.HasZeroOneRange, FABL.IsMonotoneSubsetFunction, FABL.bernoulliMarginalContribution, FABL.shapleyValue, FABL.shapleyValue_eq_integral_bernoulliMarginalContribution}
\difficulty{1}
Let $n$ be a nonnegative integer, and let $f$ be a real-valued function on the subsets
of an $n$-element set that is monotone under inclusion and takes only the values $0$ and
$1$. For every element $i$ of that set, the Shapley value of $f$ at $i$ equals the
integral from $0$ to $1$ of its Bernoulli marginal contribution as the inclusion
probability varies.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Dictator on a singleton coordinate]
\lean{FABL.shapleyDictator}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p240-b002}
\label{FABL.shapleyDictator}
\leanok
For a subset $S$ of the one-element set of coordinates, assign the value $1$ if $S$
contains its sole coordinate, and $0$ otherwise.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Monotonicity of a dictator function]
\lean{FABL.shapleyDictator_monotone}
\label{FABL.shapleyDictator_monotone}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.IsMonotoneSubsetFunction, FABL.shapleyDictator}
\difficulty{4}
For every natural number $n$, define $f$ on subsets of a one-element set by $f(S)=1$ if
its unique element belongs to $S$, and $f(S)=0$ otherwise. Whenever $S\subseteq T$, one
has $f(S)\le f(T)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Zero-one range of the dictator]
\lean{FABL.shapleyDictator_zeroOne}
\label{FABL.shapleyDictator_zeroOne}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.HasZeroOneRange, FABL.shapleyDictator}
\difficulty{4}
On the subsets of a one-element set, define the dictator function to be $1$ on subsets
containing the distinguished element and $0$ otherwise. Its values are always either $0$
or $1$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Dictator Shapley value]
\lean{FABL.shapleyValue_shapleyDictator}
\label{FABL.shapleyValue_shapleyDictator}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.shapleyDictator, FABL.shapleyValue, FABL.sum_shapleyValue}
\difficulty{3}
For the game on a single player that assigns value $1$ to a coalition containing that
player and $0$ otherwise, the Shapley value of the player is $1$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Dictator marginal contribution]
\lean{FABL.bernoulliMarginalContribution_shapleyDictator}
\label{FABL.bernoulliMarginalContribution_shapleyDictator}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.bernoulliMarginalContribution, FABL.bernoulliSubsetExpectation, FABL.shapleyDictator}
\difficulty{4}
For every real parameter $p$, the Bernoulli marginal contribution of the function on
subsets of a singleton that equals $1$ when the singleton is present and $0$ otherwise,
at its sole coordinate, is $1$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Dictator subset influence]
\lean{FABL.bernoulliSubsetInfluence_shapleyDictator}
\label{FABL.bernoulliSubsetInfluence_shapleyDictator}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.bernoulliMarginalContribution_shapleyDictator, FABL.bernoulliSubsetInfluence, FABL.bernoulliSubsetInfluence_eq_mul_marginalContribution, FABL.shapleyDictator, FABL.shapleyDictator_monotone, FABL.shapleyDictator_zeroOne}
\difficulty{1}
For every real parameter $p$, the Bernoulli subset influence of the function on subsets
of a singleton that equals $1$ when the singleton is present and $0$ otherwise, at its
sole coordinate, is $p(1-p)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Integrated influence of a dictator]
\lean{FABL.four_mul_integral_influence_shapleyDictator}
\label{FABL.four_mul_integral_influence_shapleyDictator}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.bernoulliSubsetInfluence, FABL.bernoulliSubsetInfluence_shapleyDictator, FABL.integral_pow_mul_one_sub_pow, FABL.shapleyDictator}
\difficulty{3}
For a subset $S\subseteq\{0\}$, define $f(S)=1$ if $0\in S$ and $f(S)=0$ otherwise. For
$p\in\mathbb R$, take the Bernoulli subset expectation of a function $g$ to be
$\sum_{S\subseteq\{0\}}p^{|S|}(1-p)^{1-|S|}g(S)$, and define its influence at coordinate
$0$ to be $p(1-p)$ times this expectation applied to
$S\mapsto(f(S\cup\{0\})-f(S\setminus\{0\}))^2$. Then $4\int_0^1
\operatorname{Inf}_p(f,0)\,dp=\frac23$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Shapley value and integral differ]
\lean{FABL.printed_shapley_four_integral_formula_false}
\label{FABL.printed_shapley_four_integral_formula_false}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.bernoulliSubsetInfluence, FABL.four_mul_integral_influence_shapleyDictator, FABL.shapleyDictator, FABL.shapleyValue, FABL.shapleyValue_shapleyDictator}
\difficulty{2}
On subsets of a one-element set, let $f(S)=1$ when the element belongs to $S$ and
$f(S)=0$ otherwise. Its Shapley value, defined as the expected marginal over a subset
chosen uniformly among all subsets, is not equal to four times the integral from $0$ to
$1$ of $p(1-p)$ times the Bernoulli subset expectation of the squared marginal
$(f(S\cup\{0\})-f(S\setminus\{0\}))^2$, where a subset $S$ has weight
$p^{|S|}(1-p)^{1-|S|}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Biased probability level]
\lean{FABL.biasedProbabilityLevel}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p238-b008}
\label{FABL.biasedProbabilityLevel}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.BooleanFunction, FABL.existsUnique_biasedMinusProbabilityPolynomial_eq}
Let $f$ be a monotone, nonconstant Boolean function on the $n$-dimensional cube, and let
$\alpha$ be a real number with $0<\alpha<1$. The biased probability level of $f$ at
$\alpha$ is the unique real parameter selected by the condition that the associated
biased minus-probability polynomial equals zero.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Interior biased probability level]
\lean{FABL.biasedProbabilityLevel_mem_Ioo}
\proofsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p238-b008}
\label{FABL.biasedProbabilityLevel_mem_Ioo}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.BooleanFunction, FABL.biasedProbabilityLevel, FABL.existsUnique_biasedMinusProbabilityPolynomial_eq}
\difficulty{1}
Let $f:\{-1,1\}^n\to\{-1,1\}$ be monotone and nonconstant, and let $\alpha\in(0,1)$. Let
$p_*$ be the unique number in $(0,1)$ for which the biased minus-probability polynomial
of $f$ at parameter $p_*$ equals $\alpha$. Then $p_*\in(0,1)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Value at the biased probability level]
\lean{FABL.biasedMinusProbabilityPolynomial_biasedProbabilityLevel}
\label{FABL.biasedMinusProbabilityPolynomial_biasedProbabilityLevel}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.BooleanFunction, FABL.biasedMinusProbabilityPolynomial, FABL.biasedProbabilityLevel, FABL.existsUnique_biasedMinusProbabilityPolynomial_eq}
\difficulty{1}
Let $f$ be a monotone, nonconstant Boolean function on the $n$-dimensional sign cube,
and let $\alpha\in(0,1)$. There is a uniquely specified probability parameter in $(0,1)$
at which the biased minus-probability polynomial of $f$ equals $\alpha$; at that
parameter, the polynomial indeed has value $\alpha$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Lower threshold parameter]
\lean{FABL.thresholdLowerParameter}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p238-b009}
\label{FABL.thresholdLowerParameter}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.BooleanFunction, FABL.biasedProbabilityLevel}
Let $\epsilon$ satisfy $0<\epsilon<\tfrac12$, and let $f$ be a monotone, nonconstant
Boolean function on the $n$-dimensional cube. Its lower threshold parameter is the
biased probability level of $f$ at $\epsilon$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Upper threshold parameter]
\lean{FABL.thresholdUpperParameter}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p238-b009}
\label{FABL.thresholdUpperParameter}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.BooleanFunction, FABL.biasedProbabilityLevel}
Let $\epsilon$ satisfy $0<\epsilon<\tfrac12$, and let $f$ be a monotone, nonconstant
Boolean function on the $n$-dimensional cube. Its upper threshold parameter is the
biased probability level of $f$ at $1-\epsilon$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Threshold width]
\lean{FABL.thresholdWidth}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p238-b009}
\label{FABL.thresholdWidth}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.BooleanFunction, FABL.thresholdLowerParameter, FABL.thresholdUpperParameter}
Let $\epsilon$ satisfy $0<\epsilon<\tfrac12$, and let $f$ be a monotone, nonconstant
Boolean function on the $n$-dimensional cube. Its threshold width is its upper threshold
parameter minus its lower threshold parameter.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Lower probability level]
\lean{FABL.biasedMinusProbabilityPolynomial_thresholdLowerParameter}
\label{FABL.biasedMinusProbabilityPolynomial_thresholdLowerParameter}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.BooleanFunction, FABL.biasedMinusProbabilityPolynomial, FABL.biasedMinusProbabilityPolynomial_biasedProbabilityLevel, FABL.thresholdLowerParameter}
\difficulty{1}
Let $n$ be a nonnegative integer, let $0<\epsilon<1/2$, and let $f$ be a monotone,
nonconstant Boolean function on the $n$-dimensional sign cube. The biased-minus
probability polynomial of $f$ at the lower parameter corresponding to level $\epsilon$
equals $\epsilon$; that parameter is the unique one in $(0,1)$ where the polynomial has
value $\epsilon$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Upper probability level]
\lean{FABL.biasedMinusProbabilityPolynomial_thresholdUpperParameter}
\label{FABL.biasedMinusProbabilityPolynomial_thresholdUpperParameter}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.BooleanFunction, FABL.biasedMinusProbabilityPolynomial, FABL.biasedMinusProbabilityPolynomial_biasedProbabilityLevel, FABL.thresholdUpperParameter}
\difficulty{1}
Let $n$ be a nonnegative integer, let $0<\epsilon<1/2$, and let $f$ be a monotone,
nonconstant Boolean function on the $n$-dimensional sign cube. The biased-minus
probability polynomial of $f$ at the upper parameter corresponding to level $1-\epsilon$
equals $1-\epsilon$; that parameter is the unique one in $(0,1)$ where the polynomial
has value $1-\epsilon$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Lipschitz bound for the bias variance scale]
\lean{FABL.biasVarianceScale_le_add_four_mul_abs_sub}
\label{FABL.biasVarianceScale_le_add_four_mul_abs_sub}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.biasVarianceScale}
\difficulty{4}
For real numbers $p,q\in[0,1]$, the bias variance scale at $p$, namely $4p(1-p)$, is at
most $4q(1-q)+4|p-q|$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Influence identity inside the threshold interval]
\lean{FABL.exists_thresholdInterval_influence_eq}
\label{FABL.exists_thresholdInterval_influence_eq}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.BooleanFunction, FABL.BooleanFunction.toReal, FABL.biasSigma, FABL.biasSigma_pos, FABL.biasedMinusProbabilityPolynomial, FABL.biasedMinusProbabilityPolynomial_thresholdLowerParameter, FABL.biasedMinusProbabilityPolynomial_thresholdUpperParameter, FABL.biasedProbabilityLevel_mem_Ioo, FABL.biasedSignPMF, FABL.continuous_biasedMinusProbabilityPolynomial, FABL.hasDerivAt_biasedMinusProbabilityPolynomial_eq_totalInfluence, FABL.productTotalInfluence, FABL.thresholdLowerParameter, FABL.thresholdLower_lt_critical_lt_thresholdUpper, FABL.thresholdUpperParameter, FABL.thresholdWidth}
\difficulty{6}
Let $0<\varepsilon<\tfrac12$, and let $f$ be a monotone, nonconstant Boolean function on
the $n$-dimensional sign cube. There is a bias parameter $p$ strictly between the lower
and upper threshold parameters for $f$ at error level $\varepsilon$ such that the total
influence of $f$, under the product distribution of signs with bias determined by $p$,
equals $\frac{\sigma(p)^2(1-2\varepsilon)}{w}$, where $\sigma(p)$ is the bias standard
deviation and $w$ is the difference between the upper and lower threshold parameters.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Influence bound within the threshold interval]
\lean{FABL.exists_thresholdInterval_probability_and_influence_le}
\proofsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p238-b010}
\label{FABL.exists_thresholdInterval_probability_and_influence_le}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.BooleanFunction, FABL.BooleanFunction.toReal, FABL.biasSigma_sq, FABL.biasVarianceScale, FABL.biasVarianceScale_le_add_four_mul_abs_sub, FABL.biasedMinusProbabilityPolynomial, FABL.biasedMinusProbabilityPolynomial_biasedProbabilityLevel, FABL.biasedProbabilityLevel_mem_Ioo, FABL.biasedSignPMF, FABL.criticalProbability, FABL.criticalProbability_mem_Ioo, FABL.exists_thresholdInterval_influence_eq, FABL.productTotalInfluence, FABL.strictMonoOn_biasedMinusProbabilityPolynomial, FABL.thresholdLowerParameter, FABL.thresholdLower_lt_critical_lt_thresholdUpper, FABL.thresholdUpperParameter, FABL.thresholdWidth, FABL.thresholdWidth_pos}
\difficulty{5}
Let $0<\varepsilon<\tfrac12$, and let $f$ be a monotone, nonconstant Boolean function on
the $n$-dimensional sign cube. Let $\eta>0$, and suppose $\eta$ times the bias variance
scale at the critical probability of $f$ is at most the width of its threshold interval
at error level $\varepsilon$. Then there is a bias parameter $p$ strictly between the
two threshold parameters for which the biased minus-probability lies strictly between
$\varepsilon$ and $1-\varepsilon$, and the total influence under the corresponding
biased product distribution is at most $(1-2\varepsilon)(4+1/\eta)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Recursive subsequence from a sequence]
\lean{FABL.strictSubsequenceOfNext}
\label{FABL.strictSubsequenceOfNext}
\leanok
Given a sequence $\mathrm{next}:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N$, define a sequence recursively by
$a_0=\mathrm{next}(0)$ and $a_{k+1}=\mathrm{next}(a_k+1)$ for every $k\in\mathbb N$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Positive values along a subsequence]
\lean{FABL.exists_pos_le_along_strictMono_of_nonneg_of_not_tendsto_zero}
\label{FABL.exists_pos_le_along_strictMono_of_nonneg_of_not_tendsto_zero}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.strictSubsequenceOfNext}
\difficulty{5}
Let $(a_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ be a sequence of nonnegative real numbers that does not
converge to $0$. Then there are $\beta>0$ and a strictly increasing map $\phi:\mathbb
N\to\mathbb N$ such that $a_{\phi(k)}\geq\eta$ for every $k$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Normalized threshold width]
\lean{FABL.normalizedThresholdWidth}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p238-b009}
\label{FABL.normalizedThresholdWidth}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.BooleanFunction, FABL.biasVarianceScale, FABL.criticalProbability, FABL.thresholdWidth}
Let $d$ assign a natural-number dimension to each natural number, and let
$(f_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ be a family in which $f_k$ is a monotone, nonconstant Boolean
function on the $d(k)$-dimensional cube for every $k$. For $0<\epsilon<\tfrac12$, the
normalized threshold width at $k$ is the threshold width of $f_k$ divided by the
bias-variance scale evaluated at its critical probability.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Sharp threshold property]
\lean{FABL.HasSharpThreshold}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p238-b009}
\label{FABL.HasSharpThreshold}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.BooleanFunction, FABL.normalizedThresholdWidth}
Let $d:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N$, and let $(f_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ be a family of Boolean
functions such that each $f_k$ is monotone and nonconstant on the $d(k)$-dimensional
cube. For $0<\epsilon<\tfrac12$, the family has a sharp threshold if its normalized
threshold widths converge to zero as $k\to\infty$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Coarse threshold property]
\lean{FABL.HasCoarseThreshold}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p238-b009}
\label{FABL.HasCoarseThreshold}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.BooleanFunction, FABL.HasSharpThreshold}
Let $d:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N$, and let $(f_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ be a family of Boolean
functions such that each $f_k$ is monotone and nonconstant on the $d(k)$-dimensional
cube. For $0<\epsilon<\tfrac12$, the family has a coarse threshold precisely when it
does not have a sharp threshold.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Bounded influence along a subsequence]
\lean{FABL.HasCoarseThreshold.exists_boundedInfluence_subsequence}
\proofsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p238-b010}
\label{FABL.HasCoarseThreshold.exists_boundedInfluence_subsequence}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.BooleanFunction, FABL.BooleanFunction.toReal, FABL.HasCoarseThreshold, FABL.biasVarianceScale, FABL.biasVarianceScale_nonneg, FABL.biasedMinusProbabilityPolynomial, FABL.biasedProbabilityLevel_mem_Ioo, FABL.biasedSignPMF, FABL.criticalProbability, FABL.criticalProbability_mem_Ioo, FABL.exists_pos_le_along_strictMono_of_nonneg_of_not_tendsto_zero, FABL.exists_thresholdInterval_probability_and_influence_le, FABL.normalizedThresholdWidth, FABL.productTotalInfluence, FABL.thresholdLowerParameter, FABL.thresholdUpperParameter, FABL.thresholdWidth, FABL.thresholdWidth_pos}
\difficulty{4}
Let $d_k$ be a sequence of dimensions, and let $f_k:\{-1,1\}^{d_k}\to\{\pm1\}$ be a
monotone, nonconstant Boolean function for each $k$. Fix $0<\epsilon<1/2$, and suppose
the normalized threshold widths of this family do not tend to zero. Then there are a
constant $C\in\mathbb R$, a strictly increasing sequence of indices $\phi(k)$, and, for
each $k$, a parameter $p_k$ strictly between the lower and upper threshold parameters of
$f_{\phi(k)}$, such that $\epsilon<\Pr_{p_k}[f_{\phi(k)}=-1]<1-\epsilon$ and the total
influence of $f_{\phi(k)}$ under the $p_k$-biased product measure is at most $C$.
\end{theorem}
